---
title: "Compress your first LFP recording"
---

You need Python ≥ 3.10 and a raw Neuropixels LFP binary (`.lf.cbin` or `.lf.bin`) with its
`.meta` file.

## 1. Install

```bash
uv add lfpack        # or: pip install lfpack
```

## 2. Compress

```python
from lfpack import compress_bin_to_h5

compress_bin_to_h5("my_recording.lf.cbin", "my_recording.lf.h5")
```

This runs the [pipeline](../explanation/pipeline.qmd): saturation and bad-channel
detection, filtering, decimation to 250 Hz and the codec; pass `cadzow_kwargs` to add Cadzow
denoising as IBL does; with it, a 60 min 384-channel NP1 recording gives a file of about 20 MB. Pass `cadzow_checkpoint_file=` to keep
the denoised 250 Hz array: re-running with another `alpha` then skips straight to the codec.

## 3. Read

```python
from lfpack import LFPackReader

sr = LFPackReader("my_recording.lf.h5")
print(sr.ns / sr.fs, sr.nc, sr.fs)   # duration (s), channels, 250 Hz

traces = sr[0 : int(4 * sr.fs)]      # first 4 s, (1000, nc) float32, volts
print(sr.geometry["y"])              # channel depths (µm)
```

`LFPackReader` behaves like `spikeglx.Reader`: slicing decodes only the chunks it needs.

## 4. Look at it

```bash
viewephys -f my_recording.lf.h5
```

[viewephys](https://github.com/int-brain-lab/viewephys) opens lfpack files natively.
